orders.description: Plaintiff’s limited appeal from the July 8, 2013 order granting the complaint-dismissal branch of defendants’ motion.
orders.trial_court_action: Granted summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff allegedly slipped on a yellow line painted on the ground of defendants’ premises during rain. Evidence described the line as painted about three months earlier and stated that plaintiff, who visited two or three days weekly, had not previously found it slippery.

legal_issues.finding: Defendants established noncreation of the alleged hazardous condition prima facie; plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue. The opinion relies on the painting timeline and lack of prior slipperiness but does not identify the format of those submissions.

Defendants established lack of actual notice prima facie; plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue. The opinion relies on the painting timeline and lack of prior slipperiness but does not identify the format of those submissions.

Defendants established lack of constructive notice prima facie; plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue. The opinion relies on the painting timeline and lack of prior slipperiness but does not identify the format of those submissions.

quality.notes: The fall is on expressly owned premises. BP’s name does not establish a gas station or industrial use; the ground location is other, with no inferred sidewalk/parking lot. The alleged painted-line condition is other; rain does not establish a puddle, snow/ice or storm-in-progress defense. Repeated visits support visitor role without inferring customer or employment. No exact accident date, painter identity or evidence format is supplied. The third-party caption does not change the direct negligence issue, and the fully affirmed appealed branch is label 0.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is affirmed insofar as appealed from, with costs.
The plaintiff allegedly slipped and fell when he stepped on a yellow line painted on the ground of premises owned by the defendants/third-party plaintiffs. It was raining when the accident occurred.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, the plaintiff appeals, as limited by his brief, from so much of an order of the Supreme Court, Kings County (Martin, J.), dated July 8, 2013, as granted that branch of the defendants/third-party plaintiffs' motion which was for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

The defendants/third-party plaintiffs established their prima facie entitlement to judgment as a matter of law by demonstrating that they did not create the alleged hazardous condition or have actual or constructive notice of the condition

Evidence submitted in support of the motion showed that the line had been painted about three months prior to the accident and that, prior to the accident, the plaintiff, who visited the premises two or three days a week, never found the painted line to be slippery.
In opposition, the plaintiff failed to submit evidence sufficient to raise a triable issue of fact
Accordingly, the Supreme Court properly granted that branch of the motion which was for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

orders.description: Plaintiff’s appeal from the October 30, 2017 judgment entered on the August 9, 2017 summary-judgment order.
orders.trial_court_action: Entered judgment dismissing the complaint upon granting defendant’s summary-judgment motion.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff fell while attending a luncheon in the carpeted party room of defendant’s restaurant. She alleged hazardous carpeting and testified that her left foot got stuck, but could not identify why; the asserted movement of the carpet was not established by her account.

legal_issues.finding: Plaintiff’s deposition established inability to identify the cause without speculation. It did not raise a triable issue that the carpet moved; her attorney’s opposition affirmation was also insufficient.

Law of the case barred defendant’s renewed contention that the judgment did not bring up the summary-judgment order for review, because a prior appellate motion had rejected that ground. The appeal was adjudicated on the merits; the opposition attorney affirmation did not raise a triable issue.

evidence_discussed.description: Defendant submitted plaintiff’s deposition transcript. She could not say why her foot got stuck, and her testimony did not support the alleged movement of the carpet.
Plaintiff’s attorney submitted an opposition affirmation, found insufficient to raise a triable issue; no particular reason for that insufficiency is supplied.

quality.notes: Defendant’s operation of the actual restaurant party room supports private business control without inferring ownership/lease. Luncheon attendance supports guest status; no payer/customer or tenant status is inferred. Trip mechanism is supported by the foot becoming stuck in carpeting, while the negligent cause remains unknown. Carpet is other rather than an invented uneven surface or confirmed moving rug. Only the judgment is independently appealed; the underlying order and earlier appellate dismissal-motion decision are history. Procedural law-of-case discussion is ancillary to express merits analysis. Generic creation/notice standards are not separate case-specific findings. No expert report, exact carpet defect or accident date is supplied.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the judgment is affirmed, with costs.
The plaintiff allegedly was injured when she fell at a restaurant while attending a luncheon.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, the plaintiff appeals from a judgment of the Supreme Court, Nassau County (Roy S. Mahon, J.), dated October 30, 2017. The judgment, upon an order of the same court entered August 9, 2017, inter alia, granting that branch of the defendant's motion which was for summary judgment dismissing the complaint, is in favor of the defendant and against the plaintiff dismissing the complaint.
The luncheon was held in a party room in the restaurant that had wall-to-wall carpeting on the floor. The defendant operated the restaurant.
She alleged that she fell because the carpeting in the restaurant was maintained in a dangerous and hazardous condition.

The defendant contends that the appeal from the judgment should be dismissed because the judgment does not bring up for review the portion of the order entered August 9, 2017, which granted that branch of the defendant's motion which was for summary judgment dismissing the complaint. This contention is precluded by the doctrine of law of the case.
In a decision and order on motion dated October 23, 2018, this Court denied the defendant's motion to dismiss the appeal on that ground
We agree with the Supreme Court's determination to grant that branch of the defendant's motion which was for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

Here, the defendant established its prima facie entitlement to judgment as a matter of law dismissing the complaint by submitting a transcript of the plaintiff's deposition testimony, which demonstrated that the plaintiff was unable to identify the cause of her fall
During her deposition, the plaintiff testified that she did not know what caused her left foot to get stuck on the carpeting.
Contrary to the plaintiff's contention, her deposition testimony did not raise a triable issue of fact as to whether she fell because the wall-to-wall carpeting moved.
Moreover, in opposition to the defendant's prima facie showing, the affirmation of the plaintiff's attorney was insufficient to raise a triable issue of fact

orders.description: Plaintiff’s appeal from the May 4, 2017 summary-judgment dismissal.
orders.trial_court_action: Granted defendants’ motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: Plaintiff, a tenant of defendants’ three-family home, allegedly slipped on fine, colorless black ice in front of the home on January 27, 2016. She testified that the path was clear of snow and she had not seen ice; the precise property boundary of the front path is not stated.

legal_issues.finding: Defendants established noncreation prima facie through plaintiff’s deposition and certified weather data. Plaintiff’s proposed link to negligent snow removal was speculative and raised no triable issue.
The court held the deposition and certified weather data established lack of actual notice prima facie; plaintiff raised no triable issue. It did not find that ice was impossible or never existed.
Defendants established lack of constructive notice prima facie. Plaintiff’s duration theory was speculative; the court did not specify an elapsed time or adopt a proven formation mechanism.

evidence_discussed.description: Defendants submitted plaintiff’s deposition transcript describing unseen fine/colorless black ice and a snow-free path.
Defendants submitted certified data indicating temperatures remained above freezing on the accident date; the opinion does not reproduce measurements or station details.

quality.notes: Ownership of the home is express, but in front of it and path do not establish whether the fall area was on privately owned land or an adjacent public route. Keep property review/null rather than infer either status. Walkway describes the stated path without labeling it a municipal sidewalk. Tenant status and accident date are explicit. The certified temperatures are record evidence, not a reason to erase the ice allegation. No storm-in-progress ruling or particular snow-removal method is supplied. The merits and full affirmance are clear; eligibility uncertainty concerns the accident area only.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is affirmed, with costs.
On January 27, 2016, the plaintiff allegedly was injured when she slipped and fell on ice in front of a three-family home owned by the defendants where she resided as a tenant.

In an action to recover damages for personal injuries, the plaintiff appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Kings County (Karen Rothenberg, J.), dated May 4, 2017. The order granted the defendants' motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

Here, the defendants met their prima facie burden by submitting, inter alia, a transcript of the plaintiff's deposition testimony, wherein she testified that she did not see the ice on which she slipped, which she described as "black ice," "very fine," and without color.
She further testified that the path on which she was walking prior to her fall was clear of snow and that she did not see any ice.
In addition, the certified weather data submitted by the defendants indicated that the temperature on January 27, 2016, remained above freezing.
This evidence demonstrated, prima facie, that the defendants neither created nor had actual or constructive notice of the ice that allegedly caused the plaintiff to fall
In opposition, the plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue of fact.

The plaintiff's contentions that the alleged ice condition formed as a result of the defendants' negligent snow removal efforts, or existed for a sufficient amount of time to have provided constructive notice and a reasonable time to remedy the condition, were speculative
Accordingly, we agree with the Supreme Court's determination granting the defendants' motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

orders.description: Plaintiff mother’s appeal from the May 14, 2014 summary-judgment dismissal.
orders.trial_court_action: Granted defendants’ motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.

facts.factual_summary: A child receiving physical therapy tripped over the therapist’s foot while being accompanied from the therapy room toward the waiting room. The therapist testified that the child turned abruptly after being directed toward the correct door and struck the doorway; the mother’s claim concerned negligent supervision.

legal_issues.finding: Defendants undertook supervision while requiring the mother to wait outside the therapy session and owed the child reasonable care, with the higher child-protection standard. They were not insurers required to continuously control every movement.

The court held that the sudden and unexpected movement meant any alleged supervisory inadequacy was not a proximate cause. This is a supervision-causation determination, not inability to identify the physical trip mechanism.

Defendants demonstrated adequate supervision under the undisputed accident facts; plaintiff raised no factual question in response. The court adjudicated supervision, not a defective-floor or unsafe-premises theory.

evidence_discussed.description: Physical therapist Miller described keeping the child beside her, the abrupt turn and trip over her foot, and why she had not anticipated the sudden movement. The opinion does not specify whether this was a deposition.

quality.notes: The phrase owned and/or operated does not settle ownership or private status of this institution; operator identity alone is insufficient under the initial codebook. Independently, human review should resolve whether a therapy-supervision claim arising from a trip over a therapist’s foot fits the intended private-premises negligence scope. The personal trip and substantive negligence adjudication are clear; do not mislabel this nonfall or procedural-only. The physical therapy setting is institutional and the injured role is other (patient), not the mother’s role. Defendant ownership/operation is disjunctive, so precise roles remain unclear. Hazard other is the therapist’s foot, not an invented fixed premises defect. Child status matters to the stated duty; no further demographic or injury-severity inference is recorded. The source places the therapy recommendation in 2011 but gives no full accident date. Sudden movement is not an express comparative-fault or assumption-of-risk ruling.

evidence.quote: Ordered that the order is affirmed, with costs.
She obtained the therapy at a facility owned and/or operated by defendants, and was injured when she tripped and fell there.
Appeal from an order of the Supreme Court (Ferradino, J.), entered May 14, 2014 in Saratoga County, which granted defendants’ motion for summary judgment dismissing the complaint.
Plaintiff, the child’s mother, commenced this action alleging, among other things, that defendants were negligent in their supervision of the child.
On the date in question, plaintiff was required to remain in the waiting room out of concern that she would be “a distraction” to the child during the therapy session.

Defendants undertook the duty of supervising the child under these circumstances and, as such, were “required to use reasonable care to protect the child from harm and may be liable for injury proximately caused by [their] negligence in doing so, particularly since the standard of care owed a child is higher than that required for an adult”
That being said, defendants “are not insurers of safety . . . [and] cannot reasonably be expected to continuously supervise and control all movements and activities of” a child under their care

Valerie Miller was the physical therapist who worked with the child, and the accident occurred while the two were walking from the therapy room to the waiting room so that Miller could discuss home exercises with plaintiff.

Miller testified that, as was her custom, she kept the child next to her while they were walking. When she told the child that they were going to meet plaintiff, the child became excited and forgot to turn into the waiting room. Miller then pointed out the correct door, at which point the child abruptly turned, tripped over Miller’s foot and struck her head against the corner of the doorway. Miller further testified that the child was well-behaved, and she accordingly had no reason to suspect that the child would quickly turn.

This evidence amply demonstrated that defendants provided adequate supervision for the child and that, given the sudden and unexpected nature of the child’s movements, “any alleged inadequacy in the level of supervision was not a proximate cause of the accident”
Inasmuch as plaintiff failed to raise a question of fact in response, Supreme Court properly granted summary judgment to defendants.
We affirm.
